extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and mathematicians interested in historical mathematical critique, calendrical computation, and the identification of pseudo-scientific claims
extracted.subtask_description: A mixed task: (1) identifying and critiquing pseudo-scientific or erroneous mathematical/physical claims and their rhetorical/authorial markers; (2) correctly computing the date of Easter under ecclesiastical (Gregorian) rules. The page combines historical critique with a formal algorithm for calendrical calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag claims that violate established mathematics or physics
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect and reject assertions that contradict well-established mathematical or physical principles (e.g., squaring the circle, perpetual motion, altering fundamental force laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and anti‑patterns cited: authors claiming exact quadrature of the circle (pi values like 3-1/21 or exotic algebraic expressions), perpetual motion devices (a drum half in mercury, half in vacuum 'working round forever'), or laws of gravitation stated as 'inversely as the square root' of distance. Such extraordinary claims require extraordinary proof; treat as outrageously fallacious unless supported by rigorous derivation and empirical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require stepwise derivation from established elements in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical demonstrations should proceed by gradual progression from elements, not by leaps of native intuition or unsupported manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author admonishes those who 'employ native genius upon difficulties, without gradual progression from elements'—such work often leads to error or personal ruin. Look for clear definitions, axioms, intermediate propositions, and verifiable steps; lack of these is a strong sign of invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify use of authorities and consult primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments and historical-astronomical claims should be based on direct consultation of primary sources (Clavius, Delambre, Dionysius, etc.) rather than compilers or second‑hand accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan criticizes reviewers who derive judgments from compilers and thus misstate authoritative positions. When the argument hinges on historical or technical points, check the original works (e.g., Clavius' explanations of the Calendar) to avoid being misled by novices or ignorant summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between mean (calendar) positions and true astronomical positions
rubrics_metrics.description: In calendrical reckoning, 'moon' often refers to a mean or cycle-based value (the calendar moon), not the true instantaneous position of the moon in the heavens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that ecclesiastical practice uses mean places and cycles (fictitious 'mean' sun and moon) to compute dates; the calendar moon is derived from cycles and epacts and will occasionally differ from the real full moon. Understand this distinction to interpret discrepancies and apparent 'errors' of the calendar (e.g., 1818 and 1845 cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and account for the Metonic cycle and its error
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the Metonic cycle (19 Julian years ≈ 235 lunations) is an approximation used in ecclesiastical chronology and has a built-in error (the cycle makes the mean new moons gain ~1h29m in 19 years relative to the heavens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: calendar new moons drift about a day every ~300 years. Use this knowledge when evaluating long-term calendar accuracy and when interpreting the calendar moon's relationship to the true moon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ecclesiastical cycle conventions (14th day) over literal 'full moon' when applying the calendar
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church's rules use the fourteenth day of the calendar moon (counted inclusive from the new moon of the cycle) rather than the astronomer's full moon; legal precepts that state 'full moon' may be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clavius explains that the Church 'measures only according to the order of a cycle' and treats the 14th day of the cycle as the relevant paschal marker. The correct parliamentary precept should say 'fourteenth day of the calendar moon' to reflect ecclesiastical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware false corporate or authoritative appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Skeptically evaluate pamphlets or tracts that imply endorsement by an organization or present a spurious corporate identity (e.g., 'Printed for the London Society' implying unified authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author points out that the assumption of a corporate appearance is an unfair trick and can cause public harm. Verify whether claimed societies or endorsements genuinely represent collective expert opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test doctrines by their logical and practical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author deduces prescriptive rules (e.g., religious injunctions about private provision), follow the logical implications to expose absurd or harmful consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan shows that insisting all surplus income must go to a 'Benefit Society' could be logically extended to extreme prescriptions (e.g., punishing contributors who don't pay full premiums). Use reductio ad absurdum to test doctrinal soundness and real-world feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess competence differentiation: specialist vs generalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that writers may be strong in technical specialization but weak in general learning; this affects how their mathematical claims should be managed or interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Dean Peacock: 'Murphy is a man whose special education is in advance of his general; and such men are almost always difficult subjects to manage.' When evaluating a specialist's broader claims, check for gaps in general reasoning, exposition, or social/persuasive skills that may produce errors or miscommunication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect historical doctrinal context when interpreting calendar rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding the historical and doctrinal motives (avoidance of concurrence with Jewish Passover, ecclesiastical preferences) is necessary to interpret why ecclesiastical calendar rules were chosen over strict astronomical correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clavius and others deliberately arranged cycles so that calendar moons would not coincide with Jewish reckoning; the Church sometimes prioritized liturgical and doctrinal concerns over astronomical accuracy. Evaluate calendrical rules with this context in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for determining Easter Day (Gregorian Calendar) — procedural algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: A stepwise algorithm (I–XV) to compute Easter in any year of the Gregorian calendar, involving: incrementing the year, computing quotients by 4, handling centurial corrections, dominant/ dominical letter, golden number (mod 19), epact (age of calendar moon), conditional epact adjustments, and deriving the date (day of March/April) for Easter Sunday.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives explicit steps: I. Add 1 to the year; II. quotient by 4; III. subtract 16 from centurial figures; IV. quotient of III/4; V. sum I+II+IV minus III; VI. remainder of V/7; VII. dominical letter from 7−VI; VIII. golden number from I/19 remainder; IX–X do centurial divisions; XI compute remainder of (VIII + 10×previous)/30; XII compute epact with listed adjustments; then different XIII–XIV rules depending on epact; XV combines to give day in March/April. Examples and a table of worked years are provided (e.g., year results and Easter dates). Use the provided algorithm and example table as authoritative for manual computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When epact adjustments are required, apply specified exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In computing the epact (age of the calendar moon) follow the listed special-case corrections: if epact = 0 change to 30; if epact = 24 → 25; if 25 → 26 when golden number > 11, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The algorithm enumerates exact small-number substitutions used historically to align the epact with ecclesiastical expectations. These technical corrections materially affect the computed date and must be applied exactly as stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use provided worked examples and tables to verify computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate manual calculations of Easter by comparing intermediate and final results against the supplied examples table (GIVEN YEAR row with steps I–XV and final Easter Day).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page includes a multi-column table showing intermediate values for sample years (e.g., 1592, 1637, 1723, 1853, 2018) and their final Easter dates. Use these as checks to ensure the algorithm has been implemented correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept cycles and approximations when exact astronomical computation is impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: For routine calendrical use prefer cycle-based approximations (Metonic cycle, 532-year cycle) rather than attempting to recompute true lunar positions each time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that cycles were adopted for convenience even when not perfectly accurate; periodic correction (leap-year omissions, shifts in cycle segments) is used to keep the calendar reasonable over centuries. For institutional calendrical practice, follow the established cycle rules unless undertaking a specialist astronomical recalculation.
